Kirkcaldy
kur-kaw'dee
n. (Fife burgh on the Forth, the lang toun; a Reformed salt and shipping town)
From Brittonic caer caled din, the fort on the hard hill, later read as the Scots kirk.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Kirkcaldy was a long single street of salt pans, coal heughs and shipmasters' houses along the Forth, and it reformed with the rest of Fife in 1560. It has no martyr and no synod; what it has is the ordinary Scottish parish of the century after the Reformation, in which the kirk session minuted the discipline of its members week by week, the elders visited, the heads of households were examined before communion, and family worship morning and evening was expected of every house and enquired into when it was not kept. The dictionary records Kirkcaldy as the type of that ordinary godliness, because the Scottish Reformation's real achievement was not its battles but its households. “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2) is the resolution, and the New Testament makes the government of a man's own house the test of his fitness to govern in the church.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a household as those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family, a family as the collective body of persons who live in one house under one head, and a burgh as a corporate town with certain privileges.

expand to see more

HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; a family living together.

FAMILY, n. The collective body of persons who live in one house and under one head; a race; a clan.

BURGH, n. A borough; a corporate town or village with certain privileges.

ELDER, n. One who is older; in Scripture, a person who on account of age is selected to be a ruler or officer.

Key Scripture

Psa 101:2 — "I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart."

1Ti 3:4 — "One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;"

Act 10:2 — "A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway."

Gen 18:19 — "For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment; that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him."

Modern Corruption

An ordinary reformed Fife burgh: kirk session discipline, elders' visitation, and family worship enquired into.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern privacy of the household, which makes the state of a family's worship nobody's business but its own, and so removes it from the only oversight that was ever likely to sustain it. The Scottish elders asked, and the asking is why it lasted.

The principle to recover is that the household is a unit of worship and of oversight, and that a man's rule of his own house is a public qualification. The psalmist makes it a resolution: “I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2). The eldership requires it: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity” (1Ti 3:4). Cornelius is commended by household: “A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house” (Act 10:2). And the LORD names it as the reason He chose Abraham: “he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD” (Gen 18:19).

Usage

"“One that ruleth well his own house” (1Ti 3:4) — heads of households examined before communion."

"“he will command his children and his household after him” (Gen 18:19) — family worship enquired into by the elders."
